title: Multiplexing
summary:
**Multiplexing** means carrying several independent conversations over one shared channel and separating them again at the other end. Two flavours matter:

1. **Sharing one channel.** Many senders or flows use the same medium, and something tells them apart. TCP does this at the host level: every client connects to the same `IP:port`, and the kernel demultiplexes by the full 4-tuple (see [TCP connections](#/sd/f/tcp-connection)).
2. **Sharing one connection for arbitrary byte streams.** One connection carries many logical streams. TCP gives you only an undifferentiated byte stream, so the protocol on top must add **framing** (message boundaries) and a **stream ID** in each frame. HTTP/2 and gRPC do this: hundreds of concurrent requests ride on one TCP connection as interleaved frames, bounded by the server's advertised maximum concurrent streams.

Why it matters: fewer connections means fewer handshakes (TCP and TLS), fewer ports, less memory, and warmed-up congestion windows. It is the core fix for connection and port exhaustion.

The costs: **head-of-line blocking at the TCP layer**: one lost packet stalls every stream on that connection until retransmitted (HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes this with per-stream loss recovery). And because load balancers that work at connection level see one connection, **multiplexed traffic balances unevenly** unless balancing is done per request, see [load balancing](#/sd/f/load-balancing).

drills.q: TCP delivers a stream of bytes with no message boundaries. What must a protocol add on top to multiplex several requests over a single connection?
options: Nothing; TCP already tags bytes by request
Framing plus a stream identifier in each frame
One additional TCP port per request
drills.explain: Without frames and stream IDs, the receiver cannot tell where one message ends or which request an incoming chunk belongs to. HTTP/2 frames carry exactly that.

drills.q: A client has 500 requests in flight to a server over HTTP/2. The server advertises a maximum of 100 concurrent streams per connection. What is the minimum number of connections the client needs?
drills.explain: 500 ÷ 100 = 5 connections. Over HTTP/1.1 without pipelining the same load would need about 500 connections, one per outstanding request.

drills.q: An HTTP/2 connection carries 50 streams. A single packet is lost on the network. What happens?
options: Only the stream whose data was in the lost packet pauses
All 50 streams stall until TCP retransmits the packet, because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order
drills.explain: This is TCP-level head-of-line blocking: the kernel will not hand later bytes to the application until the gap is filled. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, where loss recovery is per stream, so only the affected stream waits.

drills.q: Clients keep long-lived gRPC connections through an L4 load balancer to a backend pool. You add three new backends. Why do they receive almost no traffic?
options: The L4 balancer picks a backend once per connection, and each existing connection multiplexes all its requests to the backend it was given
gRPC does not support more than five backends
The balancer caches DNS for the new backends
drills.explain: Multiplexing concentrates many requests on one connection, and an L4 balancer only decides at connect time. Fixes: balance per request at L7, balance in the client, or have servers close connections periodically so clients re-connect.

drills.q: Give two benefits and two costs of multiplexing many requests onto one connection.
drills.answer: Benefits: fewer handshakes and ports, less memory, warmed congestion window; helps avoid ephemeral port exhaustion. Costs: TCP head-of-line blocking (one loss stalls all streams); connection-level load balancers see one connection so traffic is unevenly balanced; a single connection failure affects every stream on it.
